items.title: FLUX 3 Image Klein
items.summary: Article URL: https://bfl.ai/blog/flux-3-image-klein Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50123580 Points: 177 # Comments: 51
items.content:
Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to 10 reference images. It shares core capabilities with the full FLUX 3 Image model: native 4K generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding boxes that control where elements are placed or confine edits to a defined area.

FLUX 3 Image Klein builds on FLUX 3's shared learnings across images, video and audio. Images contribute spatial detail, video adds motion and physical dynamics, and audio provides information about events and interactions. Together, these signals help the model generate images that feel grounded in the real world.

The release includes a base model for fine-tuning and a step distilled model for low-latency generation, along with FP8, INT8 and NVFP4 builds developed with NVIDIA support, under the FLUX Kommunity License.

In internal evaluations, FLUX 3 Image Klein ranks first in text-to-image, multi-reference generation and image editing, ahead of larger open weights models. It also rates above the closed models in the comparison, Ideogram V4.5 and FLUX.2 [pro]. At 5.6B parameters, it is the smallest open model in the comparison, against 7B for Qwen-Image 2.1 and 12.9B for Krea 2. Compared with FLUX.2 [klein] 9B, it gains 91 Elo in text-to-image and 70 in image editing, with 38% fewer parameters.

FLUX 3 Image Klein was also optimized for consumer GPUs. Fewer parameters make it practical to run locally and cheaper to adapt, and teams with data sovereignty or local deployment requirements can evaluate and adapt the model on their own infrastructure. This is also key for on-device image editing, allowing consumers to edit images directly on their favorite laptops. The generator weights require 11.2 GB in BF16 and 5.6 GB in FP8. With the INT8 build, FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM, through ComfyUI or Diffusers, extending what FLUX.2 [klein] started to even smaller hardware. With the distilled model and the INT8 build, it generates a 1MP image in about 4 seconds on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070 through ComfyUI.

The base checkpoint is built for fine-tuning: Diffusers and Ostris's AI Toolkit support LoRA training from day one, and NVIDIA's NeMo AutoModel ships recipes that work directly from the released checkpoints.

For even faster production workloads that need lower latency, we also work with teams on specific customizations that get you there. Get in touch .

FLUX 3 Image Klein also extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier. Through the BFL API, it delivers lower latency than Qwen-Image 2.1, FLUX.2 [pro], Ideogram V4.5 and Krea 2, and the highest rating at its latency and above. In the charts below, the violet line traces the highest rating available at each latency and the gray line shows the previous frontier.

Latency is measured end to end, from request submission to the finished 1 MP image, including queueing. FLUX 3 Image Klein was timed on our servers. Other models were timed from the client, which includes polling and network time. Krea 2 was timed on its Medium tier; its Large tier took 31.1 seconds for text-to-image.

FLUX 3 Image Klein is available today as open weights and through the BFL API .

The weights are available under the FLUX Kommunity License, which allows free commercial use for individuals and companies with annual revenue under $5M, alongside research and non-commercial use. Larger organizations can deploy commercially through our self-hosted licensing options or API.

In an effort to make AI technology both open and safe, we implement multiple safeguards throughout the model development lifecycle to combat misuse. These include dataset filters during pre-training to limit exposure to harmful content, and targeted fine-tuning during post-training to suppress harmful behaviors, making it progressively harder to elicit harmful content. Ahead of the release, the FLUX 3 Image Klein checkpoints were rigorously red teamed internally and evaluated by our external safety partner Cinder, demonstrating substantially fewer vulnerabilities than other popular open weights models. More on our safety methodology is available here .

FLUX 3 Image Klein is the second open weights release from the FLUX 3 family, following FLUX 3 Action. More will follow.

items.title: Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network
items.summary: Speed curbs limited Ukraine's defences against deadly Russian attacks on Tuesday night.
items.content:
US President Donald Trump has denied limiting Ukraine's access to Starlink's sister internet network Starshield after it restricted drone speed, hampering Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.

"It wasn't me and I don't think it was [Starlink owner] Elon [Musk]," Trump said, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the usual speed had yet to be restored.

Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions, while news agency Reuters reported on Thursday that the order had come from inside the White House.

Ukraine was hit by several deadly strikes on Tuesday after the network slowdown.

Starlink is a civilian-use, high-speed internet network operated by Musk's SpaceX. Starshield - which relies on Starlink - is its military-grade counterpart that was designed for the Pentagon.

The US had previously warned it could withhold sharing intelligence, crucial for Kyiv's defences, if Ukraine did not stop hitting Russian oil refineries.

Tension has been brewing between Washington and Kyiv for days over a recent controversial diesel deal between Russia and the US.

Zelensky - angered by the deal - resumed targeting Russian oil refineries this week in a move criticised by Trump three days after he announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Kyiv said it would stop the strikes if Russia did the same but Moscow never confirmed the ceasefire and continued its attacks.

"If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" Zelensky asked EU leaders at a summit on Friday.

Trump had also said that Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".

But speaking to reporters as he left the White House on Friday, the US president said he had a good relationship with his Ukrainian counterpart.

Asked about Starshield, he said he was "not sure" it "ever came down".

Musk earlier explained that Starshield was managed by the US government and that the Pentagon could have been responsible.

In its report about the alleged order regarding Starshield, Reuters quoted two unnamed US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.

The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.

On Tuesday night, Starlink restricted speed limits to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.

Some 600,000 in Ukraine were left without power as communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military were also hit in the deadly attacks.

A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an investigation into the disruptions to the network.

"Restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure," the letter read.

On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron vowed that EU states would not abandon Ukraine.

Macron told a two-day summit in Brussels attended by Zelensky that it was Europe's job to hold the line in the face of some people's "ambiguities". That was apparently a reference to signs of wavering US support for Ukraine.

Funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the summit's agenda.

The war will cost €155bn (£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least €70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons.

Macron said Europe was working to help Ukraine with its satellite and early warning systems, and Ukraine's friends would look at its request for further aid.

items.title: Il papa ha chiamato Putin per chiedergli una tregua umanitaria
items.summary: Mentre era ricoverato per la rimozione del tumore al polmone: ha chiesto di permettere il passaggio di cibo e farmaci a Oleshky
items.content:
Venerdì, mentre era ricoverato al Policlinico Gemelli dopo l’intervento di rimozione del tumore al polmone , papa Leone XIV ha telefonato al presidente russo Vladimir Putin per chiedere una tregua umanitaria a Oleshky, in Ucraina.

Oleshky si trova nella regione di Kherson: è stata occupata dai russi all’inizio dell’invasione, nel 2022, e da allora è iniziata una grave crisi umanitaria che si è aggravata sempre di più: in città non ci sono elettricità, cibo, carburante, farmaci e l’unico ospedale della città è pieno di persone che non possono essere curate o di cadaveri. È da maggio di quest’anno, quindi da cinque mesi, che non arrivano consegne di cibo e medicine.

Oltre a chiedere a Putin di consentire l’arrivo di cibo e medicine, papa Leone XIV ha chiesto di permettere l’evacuazione sicura dei civili: secondo le Nazioni Unite sono rimaste bloccate all’interno della città circa 1.700 persone (circa 2mila, dice il segretario di Stato vaticano, il cardinale Pietro Parolin), la maggior parte delle quali anziane e con disabilità.

Non è la prima telefonata tra papa Leone XIV e Putin: la prima era stata a giugno del 2025, meno di un mese dopo l’elezione del papa, che da subito si è esposto per chiedere la fine della guerra in Ucraina. Dopo la telefonata il regime di Putin ha diffuso una dichiarazione in cui ha detto di essere disponibile a «collaborare» per la tregua chiesta dal papa, senza aggiungere altro né dire in che modo.

items.title: What we learned from heated US midterm Senate debates
items.summary: As the 3 November election approaches and both parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged.
items.content:
Candidates running for the US Senate in next month's midterm elections have taken to the debate stage over the past few weeks - with some heated exchanges and stinging personal attacks.

As the 3 November election approaches and parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged, particularly within some of the hotly-contested Senate races.

Republicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald Trump?

Conservatives who have bucked the president in the past have generally not fared well with voters.

The president has seen low approval ratings in recent months, with polls suggesting voters are largely concerned with the cost of living and high fuel prices.

While some Republican candidates have remained in lockstep with Trump, a Reuters analysis indicated , external that two-thirds of candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this election cycle.

Susan Collins, a Maine Republican running for her sixth term in the Senate who has repeatedly broken with Trump, is again putting clear distance between herself and the president.

"I voted with President Biden 91% of the time," Collins said during a debate last week.

"The fact is, this year alone, this Congress alone, I voted against President Trump 137 times," she said.

Collins is fighting a tighter Senate race than she expected against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. A New York Times/Siena University poll from mid-September suggests Collins could be ahead in that race by 3%, while others indicate Jackson is in the lead.

Elsewhere, some Republican candidates are choosing to separate themselves from the Trump administration's specific policy decisions, while expressing loyalty to Trump himself.

In Iowa, traditionally a Republican stronghold, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is facing a tougher-than-expected challenge in her Senate race.

She is taking on Democrat Josh Turek, and some polls suggest he has a narrow lead.

Hinson has not gone as far as Maine's Collins in separating herself from Trump, but she has broken with the president on some policy points.

During a 13 October debate with Turek, Hinson was asked about the Trump administration striking a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes to the US, followed by several other shipments.

The Republican candidate did not mince her words: "We need to lower gas prices in this country, we need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it."

NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox

As they have debated in recent weeks, the candidates haven't held back on deploying pointed personal attacks against their opponents.

The race for the vacant Michigan Senate seat - between rivals Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, and Mike Rogers, a Republican - has seen its fair share.

Rogers, a Trump-backed former congressman, questioned during a debate whether anyone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist".

El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, pushed back strongly.

He called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration" and said he was "weak, cowardly [and] won't stand up until his poll numbers drop".

On Thursday, a protester interrupted the Maine debate and Collins suggested the disrupter was associated with her opponent.

Jackson hit back at Collins: "Oh shut up, I don't even know that kid."

Further south in Georgia, more personal attacks were exchanged between incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and congressman Mike Collins, a Trump-backed Republican.

What started as an exchange where Ossoff accused Collins of taking money out of Georgians' hands to give to data centre developers, quickly turned into a hurling of insults that included Ossoff calling Collins a "bigot" who has "hired half the Third Reich".

Incendiary posts on social media from Collins' son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, have become a point of contention in the race.

In one post, Scheer blamed "Israel and Zionist Jews" for policies he said were intended to "undermine the white, Christian nature of America".

Collins defended himself by accusing Ossoff of "spewing" "craziness".

"I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don't care where the source is," the Republican said.

There are 35 Senate seats up for grabs this November, but in 21 there are no debates scheduled among the main candidates, an ABC News analysis found.

One race's lack of debates has surprised many observers: the Texas contest between James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, and Ken Paxton, a Republican and former state attorney general.

Polls in the typically Republican state suggest that Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win. Should he succeed, he could help give Democrats control of the US Senate by flipping one of the four seats they need to create a majority.

Talarico has accepted four debate invitations from different news networks. Paxton has not accepted any of those invitations.

In July, Paxton's campaign spokesperson told media outlets he would debate Talarico. But since then, the campaign and Paxton have said little on the matter.

Trump, who backed Paxton in the Republican primaries, has urged the candidates to debate.

"One thing about not showing up is you lose the opportunity to make the case for yourself, and instead, what you do is you give your opponent the ability and the opportunity to make your case as negative as possible," Peter Trumbore, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the BBC's US partner CBS News last month.

items.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
items.summary: Article URL: https://claude.dev/blog/solving-code-review-at-anthropic/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50122951 Points: 385 # Comments: 354
items.content:
How do you review code at the volume agents produce it? On the Claude Code team, once we had high coverage and deep reviews, we started optimizing for the minimum amount of human review time that doesn't raise reverts or incidents.

We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?

This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.

We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.

When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year.

Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.

This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.

We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"

Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.

Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.

So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.

A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.

Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide .

Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.

Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."

When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:

Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?

On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code , is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally.

When we launched the research preview , the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.

Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault.

Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round.

Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.

If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code .

The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here .) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it.

A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review.

The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file.

Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human.

Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves.

An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again.

The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the latest channel first. The stable channel trails it.

Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue.

Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.

One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems.

Any incidents are now an eval. The team collected past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts, and had engineers who know that code confirm each bug and where it lived. The reviewer runs against that set daily.

We measure noise by watching what people do with the comments. It's easy to catch more bugs if you don't mind flagging a lot of non-bugs, so we need a check on that. We sort every comment the reviewer leaves by how the person on the PR responded: they fixed it, said it was wrong, said the behavior was intentional, or decided it didn't matter. We also run the reviewer on PRs we know are clean and count how often it reports something that would have led someone to make a harmful change. Our priority, written down, is catching real bugs first and cutting review rounds second.

items.title: You could have invented transformers from memory
items.summary: Article URL: https://alexwang.ai/posts/associative-memory/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50122878 Points: 337 # Comments: 78
items.content:
Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world. Most recently, I was running late for a friend's board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium. It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again. We're so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted.

How do models remember so much information? And how much can they store?

In this post, I'll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store.

The key property that characterizes a "good" memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it's not very helpful if we can't recall them when we need to. The more memories we store, the more they interfere with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we'll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its capacity .

We'll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that's a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million.

Here are the terms we'll use throughout. A memory store is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A memory is one key-value pair: a key $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a value $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we query it with an input $x$, and it recalls an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an associative memory .

The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products,

where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$. 1

To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights. 2

Take a linear layer $y = Wx$ inside a network with a scalar loss $L$, and let $\bar y = \grad L(y)$ be the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer's output. The gradient with respect to $W$ is $\bar y x\transpose$, so a step with learning rate $\eta$ is

This recurrence is a memory update: it updates the weights with a new memory with key $x$ and value $-\eta\bar y$. For more on this view, see Irie, Csordás & Schmidhuber , who express a linear layer trained by gradient descent as attention over all of its training inputs.

To query the memory store with an input $x$, we multiply the input by the matrix:

So recall is a lookup by similarity to the stored keys: we compare the query with every key, and return the sum of the values weighted by those similarities.

So storing memories is easy: just keep adding outer products to the weights. But what happens when we try to recall one?

Let's assume for simplicity that every key is normalized to have length 1, i.e. $k_j\transpose k_j = 1$. Then

meaning we get back the value of the target memory , the one whose key we queried with, plus interference from every other memory whose key is similar to the query.

If the keys were all orthonormal, the interference would be zero and recall would be exact. But $\reals^{d_k}$ only has $d_k$ orthogonal directions, so we cannot get perfect recall once we store more memories than the key dimension: $M > d_k$.

What is the outer-product store's capacity? Here's an intuitive argument. There are $M-1$ interference terms. If the keys are random unit vectors, each similarity $k_i\transpose k_j$ is about $\pm 1/\sqrt{d_k}$. If the values are random too, with similar lengths, the $M-1$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference's squared length is about $(M-1)/d_k$ times the signal's, and

once we store as many memories as the key dimension, the interference is as large as the signal, drowning it out.

Each bar below is one stored memory's weight in a single recall, relative to the target memory's weight (in red). Every bar adds a bit of its value to the recall. Drag $M$ past $d_k = 64$ to watch the small bars pile up until recall fails. The other buttons switch to memory stores we'll build later in the post.

Even below its capacity of about $d_k$ memories, the outer-product store produces significant interference during recall. 3 To raise the capacity, or recall more cleanly below it, we need to reduce interference .

The brute-force way is to make the key dimension $d_k$ larger, since a linear store's capacity grows with $d_k$. How large $d_k$ can be is governed by hardware constraints.

Alternatively, we can make algorithmic improvements. We can store memories more carefully: the outer-product store adds each memory without looking at the others, so it does nothing to cancel their interference. Or we can recall more selectively: every memory in a linear store contributes interference, even when its key has low similarity to the query, so we can improve recall by suppressing the less similar keys.

In the rest of the post, we'll see that storing outer product memories more carefully gives us the optimal linear memory store, which has about twice the capacity. Recalling selectively via nonlinearities gives us MLPs and self-attention.

The outer-product store writes each memory without regard to the others. Instead, we can choose the weights $W$ so that recall fits all of the stored memories at once. This is a linear regression problem: 4

When we store more memories than the key dimension, $M > d_k$, the least-squares solution is

This is the outer-product store $V\transpose K$ with one change: before we compare the query with the keys, we multiply it by $(K\transpose K)\inverse$, which undoes the keys' covariance $K\transpose K$. This whitens the keys, so the store no longer overweights directions that many keys share.

When $M \leq d_k$, the regression can fit every memory exactly, as long as the keys are linearly independent. So the optimal store recalls with no interference at all, even when the keys aren't orthogonal.

When $M > d_k$, we start to get interference, since there are only $d_k$ directions for the memory store to work with. For random keys and values, our interference-to-signal ratio becomes

so the optimal store's capacity is twice as large as before!

When $M \leq d_k$. If the keys are linearly independent, the $M\times M$ matrix of inner products between keys, $KK\transpose$, is invertible, and

fits every memory exactly. When $M no interference and we have perfect recall.

When $M > d_k$. Setting the gradient of the objective to zero gives $W K\transpose K = V\transpose K$, so $W = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse$. Both solutions are $W = V\transpose (K\transpose)\pinv$, where $A\pinv$ denotes the pseudoinverse of $A$: $(K\transpose)\pinv = (KK\transpose)\inverse K$ when the keys are linearly independent, and $(K\transpose)\pinv = K(K\transpose K)\inverse$ when they span $\reals^{d_k}$.

Now we can analyze the interference of $f(k_j) = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$. For a stored key $k_j$, the weight on each value $v_i$ is $k_i\transpose (K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$, which is exactly entry $(i, j)$ of the $M\times M$ matrix $P = K(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose$:

$P$ is the projection onto the column space of $K$, a $d_k$-dimensional subspace of $\reals^M$. Two facts about projections help us analyze the interference-to-signal ratio:

Compared to the outer-product store's $\sqrt{M/d_k}$, the $-1$ is the $d_k$ memories' worth of interference that the optimal store cancels.

We can check our predictions numerically. We randomly sample $M$ memories with unit-length keys in $d_k = 64$ dimensions, query the memory store with one of the stored keys, and measure the interference-to-signal ratio:

The outer-product store reaches its capacity at $M \approx d_k = 64$. The optimal store recalls exactly up to $M = d_k$. Past that, its interference rises from zero like $\sqrt{M/d_k - 1}$, and the store reaches its capacity near $M = 2d_k = 128$, as predicted. Since it cancels a fixed number of memories' worth of interference, the gap between the two stores shrinks as $M$ grows.

This optimal memory store is still linear in the similarities though. It must scale small and large similarities by the same factor. To do better, we need to change how the store recalls.

If we had a way to suppress the weight when $k_i\transpose x$ is small, then we can reduce the amount of interference from low similarity keys.

items.title: Perché sono tornato ad usare un computer con Windows On Arm e Snapdragon | VIDEO
items.summary: Abbiamo usato per due anni i nuovi computer con Snapdragon e Windows On Arm. Ora con l'AI hanno tantissimo senso, ma non sono per tutti.
items.content:
Due anni fa provavo il mio primo notebook con Snapdragon X Elite e il "nuovo" Windows on ARM. Ricordo bene il video in cui ve ne parlavo, pieno di critiche e di problemi dovuti ai limiti software di quel progetto. L'hardware sembrava incredibile. Windows e le sue applicazioni non erano lontanamente pronte a supportarlo a dovere.

Nei commenti molti utenti si lamentarono, dicendo che per navigare sul web e consultare documenti andava benissimo. Vero: cose che fa praticamente ogni notebook, anche usato, da 300 euro. Se sto spendendo però 1.699 euro di listino, come per quel Samsung Galaxy Book4 Edge, permettetemi di dire che desiderare anche un utilizzo "più pro" è legittimo.

Ho continuato a utilizzare quel portatile dal 2024 a oggi, e siamo quasi al 2027. Nel tempo la situazione è sì migliorata, ma non rivoluzionata. Tantissime applicazioni, anche creative, sono arrivate in modo nativo: la tanto discussa suite Adobe compresa. Il fatto che ora girino, però, non significa che siano perfette e funzionino a dovere. Capire poi cosa funziona e cosa no non è ancora facile.

Il piu elegante di tutti? Motorola Signature, compralo al miglior prezzo da Comet.it a 802 euro.

items.title: La catastrofe umanitaria di Oleshky tra droni, mine e accuse reciproche di Mosca e Kiev
items.summary: Nella cittadina di cui hanno parlato il Papa e Putin vivono ancora 1.700 persone in condizioni critiche, intrappolate senza cibo e sotto tiro costante
items.content:
Dicono siano rimaste 1.700 anime disperse a Oleshky , la città fantasma di cui hanno parlato il Papa e Putin , infestata di droni e mine. Ci vivevano in 25mila , prima che i russi la conquistassero all’indomani dell’invasione, nel febbraio del 2022. E’ esattamente di fronte a Kherson , dall’altra parte del fiume Dnipro. Il problema dei civili, oggi, non è più solo sopravvivere ai bombardamenti: devono riuscire a trovare il pane, ma le vie d’accesso sono sotto tiro costante e i soccorsi non riescono a entrare. La Russia accusa gli ucraini di impedire i rifornimenti; Kiev denuncia il blocco delle evacuazioni da parte delle forze occupanti. Le Ong indipendenti hanno documentato una situazione umanitaria gravissima, confermata da entrambe le parti in guerra, e attacchi che tengono in costante pericolo la popolazione.

Foto e riprese recenti documentano la situazione drammatica della città, praticamente distrutta dopo quasi 5 anni di guerra. Oggi, secondo la stima di diverse fonti internazionali ci vivono ancora 47 bambini. A novembre 2022, quando le forze ucraine riconquistarono Kherson, Oleshky divenne prima linea delle forze russe che tra le marcite del Dnipro cercavano di impedire agli ucraini di attraversare il fiume per riconquistare il sud in direzione della Crimea. Da una parte del fiume c’erano le linee ucraine, dall’altra quelle russe. E da entrambe le parti, nel capoluogo Kherson come nella piccola Oleshky, continua a scorrere il sangue dei civili.

Iscriviti a " La sottile linea rossa ", la newsletter di Gianluca Di Feo

Nel giugno 2023 l’inondazione provocata dalla distruzione della diga di Kakhovka - di cui russi e ucraini si rimpallano le responsabilità, ma inchieste come quella New York Times basate su riscontri tecnici propendono per assegnare la colpa ai primi - ha devastato anche Oleshky. L’isolamento della città è peggiorato progressivamente dall’anno scorso, per l’aumento drammatico di droni e la presenza di bombardamenti e mine .

L’Onu ha riscontrato grave scarsità di cibo e assistenza medica, strade e percorsi minacciati da mine e droni, attacchi contro civili e soccorritori, ambulanze che non riescono più a raggiungere regolarmente le case, malati e feriti che non possono essere evacuati. Dall’inizio dell’anno, secondo un rapporto Onu di fine giugno, a Oleshky e Hola Prystan - un altro paese di frontiera poco più giù lungo la sponda sinistra del fiume – sono stati uccisi almeno 29 civili. Ma Oleshky non è solo un fronte di guerra, è anche un perfetto teatro di scontro della propaganda . Il rapporto Onu riconosce che il suo territorio controllato dalle forze russe è percorso da droni lanciati dalle forze ucraine, e descrive attacchi come quello del 5 marzo contro persone in fila per ricevere cibo. A maggio, un attacco ha ucciso un soccorritore e un uomo intervenuto ad aiutarlo. Ma precisa di non avere potuto attribuire con certezza le responsabilità di ogni singolo attacco. Accanto ai civili e lungo le sponde del fiume si annidano le posizioni russe da cui partono gli attacchi quotidiani a Kherson, che gli ucraini definiscono “safari umano” accusando i russi di inseguire e uccidere deliberatamente i civili. E la situazione alimentare , raccontata da familiari di persone rimaste a vivere lì, è gravissima. La fame, e il rischio concreto di morirne, sono documentati. Russi e ucraini se ne rimpallano la responsabilità. Per il Cremlino la città è sotto un blocco imposto dall'Ucraina con droni, bombardamenti e mine che impediscono di ripristinare i servizi essenziali. Per Kiev è la Russia ad aver trasformato la città in una trappola, limitando le evacuazioni e l’accesso agli aiuti e impedendo agli abitanti di fuggire raggiungendo luoghi sicuri. L’Ucraina ha proposto tregue locali e organizzato consegne di cibo con i droni, ma accusa i russi di aver fatto di tutto per ostacolarle.

Vladimir Saldo , capo dell’amministrazione regionale russa nel territorio occupato, la scorsa settimana ha detto che Mosca avrebbe accolto proposte concrete capaci di ridurre le ostilità e migliorare le condizioni di vita degli abitanti, criticando la “campagna propagandistica internazionale” sul caso Oleshky e sostenendo che la maggior parte dei civili rimasti abbia scelto autonomamente di restare nella propria casa. Sostiene che dall’inizio dell’anno gli attacchi ucraini abbiano ucciso 68 civili nel distretto, di cui 29 in città. Il ministero degli Esteri russo accusa Kiev di usare i droni per bloccare la città attaccando i convogli umanitari.

Dmytro Lubinets , difensore civico ucraino, sostiene che Kiev abbia proposto alla Russia una tregua locale per evacuare i residenti, senza ottenere l’autorizzazione russa necessaria. Se ne parlava apertamente già a maggio, ma non si riuscì a organizzare un’evacuazione generale. Tetiana Hasanenko, responsabile dell’amministrazione municipale trasferita sul territorio controllato da Kiev, denuncia la distruzione quasi completa della città e dice che molti cittadini sopravvivono con scorte minime e non possono uscire senza rischiare la vita. Il ministro degli Esteri ucraino Sybiha attribuisce alla Russia la piena responsabilità della catastrofe e ha portato la questione nelle sedi internazionali, sostenendo che la Russia controllando il territorio abbia la responsabilità di assicurare la sopravvivenza degli abitanti.

Un rapporto di luglio di Human Rights Watch basato su interviste a residenti fuggiti conferma la situazione gravissima descrivendo però attacchi ucraini prolungati nella zona; e ha trovato “indizi credibili” di mine e droni ucraini anche sulle strade di Oleshky. Il 25 settembre un militare della 34ª brigata ucraina ha ammesso a Ukrainska Pravda che Kiev mina a distanza alcuni percorsi per impedire i rifornimenti militari russi, sostenendo però che la strada principale viene lasciata libera per i civili.

items.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
items.summary: https://words.filippo.io/seeds-solved/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50122800 Points: 913 # Comments: 338
items.content:
“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.

We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.

Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.

ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information where it came from.

Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “ A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma ”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them .

The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:

Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.

Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.

In under half an hour , Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!

The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp ( t ) for some number of iterations ( n ). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1842 iterations to output the standardized seed.

This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.

Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state.

Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator lrand48 , which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.

The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.

This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48 , with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.

However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.

But wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?

While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3 and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in FreeLIP , Arjen Lenstra 's long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of Victor Shoup 's NTL library shipped the same code.

Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507 and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.

As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.

Not every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.

Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.

There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves.

The $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the Internet Security Research Group .

This work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis.

We would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “ evil Internet meme ” and the “ Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen ” with good humor. Also thanks to Filippo Valsorda for organizing the NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty.

items.title: Llama.cpp on a jailbroken PS5: run any GGUF model natively on the console
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/cobanov/PS5LM Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50122431 Points: 307 # Comments: 75
items.content:
Your PS5 runs the language model. Every device on your network uses it. llama.cpp on the console's GPU, with OpenAI and Anthropic APIs and a screen made for the TV.

New: decision models, powered by Ollaya . PS5LM now runs Jev-like decision models (d1, Clef, OpenJev and more) on the GPU and answers the same /v1/systemone API as Ollaya: typed decisions with calibrated probabilities, in a fraction of a second.

PS5LM is for anyone with a jailbroken PS5 who wants a private model server at home. It loads a GGUF model onto the console's GPU and serves it to your laptop, your phone and your coding tools. It needs no PC while it runs, no cloud and no account.

Qwen 3.5 9B answering requests from a laptop on a PS5 Slim. Click for the video.

Ollaya runs open decision models on a PC the way Ollama runs language models. PS5LM brings the same idea to the console: a decision model reads a state and answers typed questions in one forward pass, with no text generated.

The Suggested list has d1 Omni 600M, d1 3B and Clef Flash. Any GGUF that carries llama.cpp's decision metadata loads the same way, and the app labels it a decision model.

You need a PS5 on firmware 7.00 to 13.60, jailbroken, with these payloads loaded:

To update, copy the new folder over the old one. Settings, models and downloads stay in /data/PS5LM . Using it from coding tools (opencode, Codex, Claude Code) is in docs/CLI.md .

C++ on ps5-homebrew-ui , llama.cpp with ggml-vulkan on PS5_Vulkan 's RADV, built on Linux.

Building · Console notes · Porting · Research · Models that fit · Roadmap · Changelog · The original payload

GPL-3.0-or-later, see LICENSE . llama.cpp keeps its MIT licence, Manrope its OFL. No Sony SDK files, keys, firmware or model weights are in this repository.

items.title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
items.summary: The Australian government hopes to protect social media users from being served content they don't want to see.
items.content:
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder

Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.

It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.

Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.

Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.

It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.

He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.

"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."

The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.

Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."

Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.

Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.

But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction , external ; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health , external , and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline .

Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.

While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.

"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.

More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.

"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.

"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."

Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram, US court hears

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m).

"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.

There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.

In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise .

"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.

Right-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.

But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.

The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.

However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban ? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.

The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.

Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.

"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation , external .

On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.

items.title: eBay Restricts Listings of Radio Equipment, but Exempts Ham-Band-Only Gear
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.arrl.org/arrlletterissue?issue=2026-10-15#eBay-Restricts-Listings-of-Radio-Equipment_-But-Exempts-Ham-Band-Only-Gear Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50122034 Points: 233 # Comments: 210
items.content:
Florida Hams Provide Communications Support During Hurricane Isaias

eBay Restricts Listings of Radio Equipment, but Exempts Ham-Band-Only Gear

Florida Hams Provide Communications Support During Hurricane Isaias

Amateur radio operators from Florida’s Santa Rosa, Nassau, Lake, Pinellas, and Leon Counties played an important role in supporting emergency communications efforts during and following Hurricane Isaias, helping ensure that critical communication capabilities remained available throughout the storm.

In Santa Rosa County, volunteer amateur radio operators staffed the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) and the evacuation shelter at the Milton Community Center. These volunteers provided a communications link between the shelter and the EOC, relaying situational updates and maintaining readiness to support emergency communications should traditional systems become unavailable.

Amateur radio operators across the state also supported auxiliary communications efforts, providing additional capabilities to maintain contact with the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee if conventional communication networks experienced disruptions.

"While traditional communications systems have become significantly more reliable over the years, amateur radio continues to serve as a dependable auxiliary communications resource," said Arc Thames, W4CPD, Santa Rosa County Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) and Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES) Program Manager. "When disaster strikes, our volunteers are trained, prepared, and ready to step in wherever we're needed. It's another layer of resiliency that helps protect our communities."

Thames also serves as the ARRL Northern Florida Section Emergency Coordinator and the Amateur Radio Liaison to the Florida Division of Emergency Management, supporting the coordination of amateur radio and auxiliary communications resources statewide.

"During tropical weather events impacting Florida, our Auxiliary Communications team provides volunteer operators to monitor amateur radio communications at the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee," Thames explained. "This ensures that if someone is unable to reach emergency officials through traditional means, we have another way to receive and relay critical information. We always hope we're not needed, but we're glad to be there just in case when all else fails." — Thanks to ARRL Northern Florida SEC Arc Thames, W4CPD, for the above

eBay Restricts Listings of Radio Equipment, but Exempts Ham-Band-Only Gear

Online marketplace eBay has imposed new restrictions on listings of radio transmitting equipment in response to new FCC rules that took effect this week, but responded to ARRL that its new policy will not apply to gear that operates exclusively on amateur radio frequencies . The FCC’s rules are intended to use its equipment authorization program to protect against “national security threats to the communications supply chain” and cover a wide variety of products.

In its Third Report and Order issued on July 23, 2026, the Commission makes clear that online marketplaces share in the legal responsibility to assure that unauthorized RF devices are not offered for sale on their platforms. The rules took effect on October 13. Moving forward, equipment subject to FCC authorization must have its FCC ID number submitted to the marketplace and posted with its listing. There are exemptions for posts already online, “small sellers,” and used equipment, but initial messages to sellers from eBay suggested that an FCC ID would be required in order to post a listing for any equipment that transmits RF energy.

In response to a request from ARRL for a clarification relating to amateur radio equipment that does not require FCC authorization, an eBay spokesperson provided the following statement:

eBay allows the sale of devices capable of operating only on frequencies that the FCC has allocated for use by Amateur Radio Service licensees. As these devices do not require FCC equipment authorization, FCC IDs will not be required for these listings as an amateur licensee may use his or her license to operate such radios. However, two-way VHF/UHF radio equipment capable of operating outside of the amateur frequency bands cannot be imported, advertised, sold, or operated within the United States, including on eBay, without an FCC equipment certification. If eBay inadvertently takes action against listings for devices that don't require FCC IDs and are otherwise authorized, the affected seller should inform eBay and we will assess whether to remove restrictions from the listing.

It should be emphasized that the FCC did not change its underlying equipment authorization rules. Amateur radio equipment, except for commercial HF amplifiers, continues to not require FCC authorization.

The Radio Club of America has brought together both wireless industry professionals and amateur radio operators for more than 100 years. Each year, it bestows prestigious awards and elevates several members to RCA Fellows. This year, as always, many of those on the list are hams. The award recipients include Dr. Charles C. Counselman, III, W1HIS, who developed technology for making highly accurate GPS positioning widely available; Jay Adrick, K8CJY, who helped develop digital television and serves as Board President of the National Voice of America Museum of Broadcasting; inventor Charles Kirmuss, WØCBK, who developed digital video and audio recording systems for public safety; Carole Perry Young Professional Award winner and electrical engineer Audrey McElroy, KM4BUN, a longtime proponent of youth in amateur radio; Dr. Ajay Poddar, AC2KG, an internationally-recognized leader in radio science and engineering; Dr. Henry Richter, W6VZA (SK), who developed the communications system for Explorer 1, the first US Earth satellite; and Anthony Rizi, NR1Z, a military and cybersecurity professional and college professor who is also active in ARISS, the Amateur Radio on the International Space Station program.

This year’s class of RCA Fellows include amateurs Rachel Jones, KO4HLC; Geoffrey Mendenhall, W8GNM; Nick Pennance, N1CKP, and Dominic “Nick” Tusa, K5EF. The award winners and new Fellows will be formally recognized at RCA’s 2026 Technical Symposium and Awards Banquet in New York City on November 21. Visit the club’s website for a complete list of awardees and their biographies .

Back in the earliest days of the internet, a whole block of IP (internet protocol) addresses — beginning with 44 — was set aside for amateur radio use. Most of that block of addresses is still there and is managed by ARDC, Amateur Radio Digital Communications. In December of 2025, ARDC launched 44Net Connect, a service intended to make it easy for hams to begin using 44Net addresses for such things as experimenting with digital modes, improving repeater infrastructure, setting up a home lab, and more. In the ensuing months, more than 2000 users have signed up and ARDC is now expanding access by doubling its number of “points of presence,” or “PoPs” around the world, adding new ones in Chicago, Los Angeles, and Sydney, Australia (current ones are in Frankfurt, Toronto, and Dallas). A PoP is a physical access point that connects different networks. “The additional PoPs will expand network capacity and bring nodes closer to users in different parts of the world,” explained Rebecca Key, KO4KVG, ARDC’s Communications Manager. “This can shorten the distance data travels, reducing latency, and improving the overall experience.”

“44Net Connect gives licensed hams a simpler way to get a static 44Net IP address without a complicated setup,” adds Key. “We’re seeing it used for everything from personal tinkering to club projects, education, and EmComm.”

You can find more information about 44Net Connect, including how to get started, in ARDC’s introductory blog post .

Mel Parkes, NM7P, has resigned as Vice Director of the ARRL Rocky Mountain Division, effective October 10, 2026. Parkes was elected in 2025 to a three-year term that began January 1, 2026. He cited health and personal reasons for his resignation.

Previously, Parkes served as Utah Section Manager for 22 years, from 1999 until 2021.

ARRL President Rick Roderick, K5UR, has appointed Ed James, KA8JMW, of Edgewood, New Mexico, to be the new Vice Director, serving the remainder of Parkes’ term, which runs through December 31, 2028. An ARRL Life Member, James has served in multiple ARRL Field Organization positions, including Section Manager of New Mexico.

ARRL is governed by an all-volunteer Board of Directors. Elections are held annually for five of ARRL’s 15 Divisions, with Directors and Vice Directors serving 3-year terms.

items.title: RetroBox Modem è il progetto perfetto per i nostalgici degli albori del Web
items.summary: Estetica anni Novanta e tutti quei bei suoni che facevano i modem dell'epoca.
items.content:
Se qualcuno ha nostalgia dei tempi in cui internet non funzionava se qualcuno parlava al telefono - e faceva anche parecchio rumore quando si attivava (perché no, non era 24/7, a meno di essere veramente, veramente ricchi), un appassionato di elettronica ha il progetto basato su Raspberry Pi che fa al caso vostro: si chiama RetroBox Modem, ed è un vero e proprio modem fai-da-te Wi-Fi, compatibile con lo standard Hayes e pensato per accedere ai servizi BBS (Bulletin Board System, altro pezzo fondamentale della preistoria del Web) ancora attivi.

A differenza dei semplici adattatori seriali-Wi-Fi, il dispositivo riproduce diversi comportamenti dei modem tradizionali, compresi i comandi AT, le sequenze di composizione del numero, gli indicatori di stato della connessione e i caratteristici suoni della negoziazione. Alla base di tutto il progetto troviamo un Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, che gestisce la connessione Wi-Fi, le comunicazioni di rete e l'interprete dei comandi Hayes. Il computer collegato invia istruzioni come AT e ATD attraverso una porta seriale; RetroBox le traduce in connessioni TCP/Telnet, consentendo di raggiungere i BBS senza bisogno di una vera linea telefonica.

Il piu elegante di tutti? Motorola Signature, compralo al miglior prezzo da Comet.it a 802 euro.
